newsitem.title: USA: IMF's Camdessus upbeat on world economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Camdessus upbeat on world economic outlook.

text.p: International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus Tuesday delivered an upbeat assessment of the global economic outlook, but warned that problems remained.

Kicking off the plenary session of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting, Camdessus ticked off a variety of factors for the improved outlook, including currency rates more closely in line with fundamentals and low inflation.
"World economic and financial conditions are generally satisfactory and the outlook is favorable," Camdessus said.

"Among the more positive developments, I would cite the reduction in world inflation," Casmdessus said. "In particular, many industrial countries have come close to achieving effective price stability."
Developing countries are also enjoying solid growth.

The recovery in Latin America is gaining momentum, Africa appears to be "on the move" after decades of lagging behind, and growth in Asia is slowing to more sustainable, yet still impressive, rates, he said.
"The countries in transition that were thrust into a brave new world are no longer dazed and have begun their upward climb," Camdessus added.
But that does not mean that the world economy is free of problems.
"Yes, there have been many positive developments in the global economy," Camdessus said. "Yet, we also know that macroeconomic and structural weaknesses persist in all of our countries."
The IMF chief called fragile national banking systems the "Achilles heel" of the global economy. "In many countries, a banking crisis is an accident waiting to happen," he said.
He called on IMF member nations to launch a more ambitious attack on their budget deficits and adopt a bolder approach to structural economic reforms.

"In every country, we can point to ways in which comprehensive structural reform -- not just tinkering at the margin with this measure or that -- would improve the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies (and) help create jobs," Camdessus said.

Camdessus told the plenary session that the IMF itself will need more money so that it can play its part in helping member nations carry out the needed, painful reforms and sheltering the world economy from crises when they occur.
"Since it is unlikely we will be able to avert every crisis, we must equip ourselves to face unexpected, and potentially disruptive, developments," he said.

He welcomed the progress that industrial countries have made in talks with up-and-coming developing countries about doubling the IMF's emergency resources. That arrangement is about to be finalized, he added.
He also called for rapid agreement among the IMF's 181 member nations on a plan to boost the Fund's capital through a so-called quota increase.
"This truly will be a critical priority in the coming months," he said.
Camdessus has called for a doubling of the IMF's capital base, but some industrial nations remain wary of such a big increase.
